title: How to verify a vendor before you pay them
summary: A real supplier can be impersonated and a fake one can look real. The checks that separate them, what each one proves, why a change of bank details is the…
body_markdown:
Treat the request as unverified until you have called the vendor on a phone number you already hold, from your vendor file, the contract or an invoice you have already paid, and not one given in the request. Ask someone you have dealt with before to confirm the old account, the new one and the reason. Hold any payment to the new account until that call is done, have a second person approve the change, and use your bank's account-name check if it offers one.


Check that it matches a real order and delivery, that it came from the email domain in your vendor file, and that the bank details on it are the ones you have paid before. An invoice that changes the payment account, comes from a domain registered recently or presses for urgent payment should be confirmed by calling the vendor on a number you already hold. A matching sender address is not proof, because a vendor's own mailbox can be compromised.


Business email compromise, or BEC, is a scam in which criminals compromise or impersonate email accounts and other channels to trick a business into transferring funds. A common form targets businesses that pay suppliers by asking for the payment to go to a new account. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center received 24,768 BEC complaints in 2025, with reported losses of just over $3 billion.


Look the company up in the registry where it says it is registered and check its status, its address and, where the registry lists them, its officers. Then check that the people who sign its emails exist and work there, that its email domain is not new or a lookalike of a known brand, and that other customers, reviews, trade bodies and news have recorded it over time. A registry entry shows the company was filed, so the footprint is what shows it trades.


Call your bank at once on its official number, ask it to recall the payment and give it the full transaction details. The IC3's advice is that "time is of the essence". In the US, file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center whatever the amount, and in England, Wales and Northern Ireland report to Report Fraud, or to Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Keep the emails with their headers, and tell the real vendor, whose mailbox may have been compromised.


No. A lookalike domain can differ by one character, and when a vendor's real mailbox is compromised the email comes from the right address and often from inside a real thread. A callback on a number you already hold is the check that works in both cases.
